sections.h2: How a Missouri beneficiary deed works
sections.html:
Missouri's version is called a beneficiary deed, and it hands real estate to a named person at the owner's death without a probate case for that property. Section 461.025 of the Nonprobate Transfers Law describes it as a deed to a designated grantee that says outright that it does not take effect until the owner dies.

Two conditions make it work. The deed has to be signed and filed of record, before the owner's death, in each county or city where the land lies. And it must contain the express statement that it takes effect only on death. The deed needs no consideration and need not be delivered to the beneficiary, and the beneficiary can be a trust whether or not the trust is revocable.

A deed that is not recorded until after the owner's death is not automatically void. Section 461.025 leaves intact any deed that is otherwise effective by law to pass title, even if recorded late. The beneficiary deed itself, though, only qualifies under this section when it is filed before death.

sections.h2: Can the owner still sell or change the property while alive?
sections.html:
Yes. The beneficiary gets no rights in the property during the owner's lifetime, and the beneficiary's signature is never needed for anything the owner wants to do with the house. That rule is in section 461.031.

The rules for changing or cancelling the designation sit in section 461.033:

  • An owner may revoke or change a beneficiary designation in whole or in part at any time before death.
  • When joint owners are involved, a change needs the agreement of every owner still living.
  • A later designation replaces an earlier one unless it says otherwise.
  • A will cannot undo a beneficiary designation unless the designation itself gave the owner the right to revoke by will.
  • Selling or giving away the property during life ends the designation for that property.

The last point is the one a seller cares about. A recorded beneficiary deed does not stop you from listing the house, taking a cash offer and closing, and the sale ends the beneficiary's claim to the parcel sold.

sections.h2: What happens to the property when the owner dies
sections.html:
The house passes by operation of law to the beneficiary, with no court order needed for the transfer itself (section 461.031). If two or more beneficiaries survive, they hold separate shares as tenants in common, and no survivorship right runs between them unless the deed expressly provides one. A share belonging to a beneficiary who later dies goes to that person's estate.

When no beneficiary survives the owner, the property belongs to the owner's estate instead. Where joint owners made the designation together, the surviving joint owner takes the property when the first one dies.

How the beneficiary deed behaves in common Missouri situations
SituationResult
Owner lives onBeneficiary has no rights in the property
Owner dies, beneficiary survivesProperty passes to beneficiary by operation of law
Two beneficiaries surviveTenants in common unless survivorship is stated
No beneficiary survivesProperty belongs to the owner's estate
Owner divorces after signingProvision for former spouse and spouse's relatives is revoked
Owner sells the houseDesignation ends for the parcel sold

Both can affect the deed. Under section 461.051, if the owner's marriage ends in divorce or annulment after the designation, any provision in favor of the former spouse, or of a relative of the former spouse, is revoked on the date the marriage ends. The designation is read as though that person had disclaimed. The revocation does not apply if the designation was made irrevocable, was made after the divorce, or says expressly that a divorce does not affect it. Remarrying the former spouse revives the provision.

Creditors keep some reach. Section 461.071 gives a deceased owner's creditors, surviving spouse and unmarried minor children the rights set out in section 461.300 against the value of property that passed outside probate. A beneficiary who receives a house may be asked to contribute toward statutory allowances and claims if the probate estate cannot cover them.

Anyone who inherits a house this way and plans to sell it quickly should ask the probate division clerk in the county whether any estate has been opened, since an open estate or a creditor claim could slow the closing.

sections.h2: When a small estate affidavit can replace a deed
sections.html:
If no beneficiary deed exists and the whole estate is small, heirs may claim the real estate with an affidavit instead of a full administration. Section 473.097 sets the test:

  • The estate, after subtracting liens, debts and encumbrances, is worth no more than $40,000.
  • A month has gone by since the death, and nobody has applied for letters or been granted them.
  • The person making the affidavit files a bond approved by the probate judge or clerk, unless the court decides a bond is unnecessary.
  • The filing fee set by section 483.580 is paid, along with any required creditor notice publication cost.

The affidavit itemizes the property with values, names the people who will receive each item, and swears that debts will be paid. The clerk attaches a certificate. Heirs then prove their right to real estate by recording both papers in every county that holds a piece of it. If the itemized property tops $15,000, the clerk runs a creditor notice in a local paper for two straight weeks.

Property that the decedent held as a tenant by the entirety or joint tenant is left out of the affidavit's list. An estate above the $40,000 limit does not qualify, which is one reason owners record a beneficiary deed while they are alive.

After title transfers, the beneficiary owns the property outright and can sell it like any other owner. A buyer's closing agent will want the recorded beneficiary deed and proof that the former owner has died. Ask the county recorder what they require to place a death certificate or similar proof on record in your county.

Where the owner left no deed, the heirs usually need a probate case or a small estate affidavit first. Our Missouri recording guide explains page format, fees and acknowledgment for the deeds that will follow, and the Missouri probate laws page covers what happens when an estate has to be opened.

Check the property tax bill early. Learn the parcel's current tax balance from the county collector before any offer is signed. A cash sale skips repairs and buyer financing, so a beneficiary who lives elsewhere can often close once the recorded deed and death proof are in the title company's hands.

faqs.q: Does a Missouri beneficiary deed skip probate?
faqs.a: For the property it names, yes. Under section 461.025 the house passes to the designated beneficiary at the owner's death when the deed was on file beforehand. Other assets may still need probate.

faqs.q: Must the beneficiary sign or accept a Missouri beneficiary deed?
faqs.a: No. The deed needs no consideration and need not be delivered to the beneficiary, and the beneficiary's signature is never required for the owner's transactions.

faqs.q: Can I cancel a Missouri beneficiary deed?
faqs.a: Yes, at any time before death. Section 461.033 lets the owner revoke or change it, though joint owners must all agree, and a will cannot revoke it unless the deed allows that. A later designation replaces the earlier one.

faqs.q: What if the beneficiary dies before the owner in Missouri?
faqs.a: The designation fails for that person. If no beneficiary survives the owner, the property belongs to the owner's estate, which then goes through the usual estate process.

faqs.q: How big can a Missouri estate be for the small estate affidavit?
faqs.a: The value of the entire estate, less liens, debts and encumbrances, may not exceed $40,000. Section 473.097 also requires a thirty-day wait after the death and no pending application for letters.
